extracted.intended_audience: general public; researchers, journalists, and potential grantees interested in the Gates Foundation and its grantmaking policies
extracted.subtask_description: Encyclopedic summary of the Gates Foundation's organization, program priorities, funding commitments, grantmaking policies, reporting practices, and program-specific requirements (e.g., Reinvent the Toilet challenge, Grand Challenges). Useful for understanding how the foundation funds, reports, and constrains grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-access (OA) policy for publications and data
rubrics_metrics.description: The foundation adopted an open-access (OA) policy "to enable the unrestricted access and reuse of all peer-reviewed published research funded by the foundation, including any underlying data sets." Its terms have been called the most stringent among similar OA policies; effective for all new agreements as of January 1, 2015.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gates Open Research was based on the Wellcome Trust initiative and launched with F1000 Research. In 2024 the foundation announced a "preprint-centric" open access policy and an intention to stop paying article-processing charges. The foundation has supported open-access outlets (e.g., Our World in Data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private foundation payout requirement (minimum annual distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: To maintain its status as a charitable foundation, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation must donate funds equal to at least five percent of its assets each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The foundation posts audited financial statements and 990-PF forms publicly. The five-percent payout requirement is stated as a condition for charitable status and affects annual grantmaking budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warren Buffett donation conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Buffett set conditions for his Berkshire Hathaway stock contributions: Bill or Melinda Gates must be alive and active in its administration; it must continue to qualify as a charity; and each year it must give away an amount equal to the previous year's Berkshire gift, plus an additional amount equal to 5 percent of net assets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conditions effectively made Buffett's gifts function as matching contributions that influence the foundation's annual disbursements; the gifts were delivered as scheduled shares over multiple years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant reporting transparency and IATI participation (scope and exclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The foundation maintains an online database of grants and announced in October 2013 that it would join the International Aid Transparency Initiative (IATI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IATI publications include only a subset of Gates Foundation grants (mainly excluding grants to developed countries and few grants before 2009). The foundation states: "reporting starts from 2009 and excludes grants related to our US programs and grants that if published could harm our employees, grantees, partners, or the beneficiaries of our work." Committed funding tables and top recipient lists are published in IATI-derived outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinvent the Toilet Challenge technical and contextual criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The Reinvent the Toilet Challenge aimed to create a toilet that removes pathogens, recovers resources (energy, clean water, nutrients), operates "off-the-grid" without connections to water, sewer, or electrical networks, and costs less than 5 cents per user per day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program explicitly excluded project ideas that relied on centralized sewerage systems or were not compatible with developing-country contexts. Typical grant sizes: first-round ~ $400,000, second-phase typically $1M–$3M. The challenge emphasized both high-tech and low-tech solutions appropriate for low-resource settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: WASH program strategic funding focus
rubrics_metrics.description: As of mid-2011 the foundation refocused WASH (Water, Sanitation and Hygiene) funding mainly on sustainable sanitation services for the poor and less on water supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since 2011 grant-making in WASH prioritized: sanitation science and technology ("transformative technologies"), delivery models at scale, urban sanitation markets, building demand for sanitation, measurement and evaluation, and policy/advocacy/communications. The foundation reported committing >$265 million over a five-year period and around $650 million between ~2008–2015 to WASH projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement/expectation for research result sharing among funded teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Some funding programs required that awardees share findings with other funded teams—for example, HIV research funding of $287 million was split between 16 different research teams on the condition that the findings be shared among the teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects programmatic expectations that grantees collaborate and disseminate results across funded networks rather than siloed proprietary research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand Challenges Explorations (GCE) and phased grant model
rubrics_metrics.description: Grand Challenges Explorations awarded early-stage grants of $100,000 each in the first round (2011–2013) with follow-on larger funding available for promising projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Grand Challenges approach funds high-risk, high-reward ideas with small initial grants and larger subsequent awards for successful early-stage projects (examples: Reinvent the Toilet follow-on amounts; Grand Challenges in Global Health follow-ons up to ~$1M).

rubrics_metrics.name: Program-specific design criterion example — Next-Generation Condom
rubrics_metrics.description: The Next-Generation Condom grant competition sought condoms that "significantly preserves or enhances pleasure, in order to improve uptake and regular use."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows programmatic selection criteria focused on behavioral uptake and product acceptability in addition to biomedical effectiveness; initial small grants (e.g., $100,000) were used to seed prototype development with potential for larger follow-on awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant suitability for developing-country contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Several Gates programs explicitly required that proposed solutions be compatible with developing-country contexts and excluded ideas dependent on infrastructure unlikely to exist in those settings (e.g., centralized sewerage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs like Reinvent the Toilet and Grand Challenges prioritized off-grid, low-cost, easily deployable solutions; reviewers and program officers rejected proposals that relied on unrealistic assumptions about infrastructure in target countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation organizational/program priorities (program area criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: The foundation is organized into program areas (Global Development Division, Global Health Division, United States Division, Global Policy & Advocacy Division, Global Growth & Opportunity Division) through which it sets strategic priorities and monitors results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program leadership (set by CEO) defines which thematic areas and modalities are prioritized for grantmaking and partnership; grantees are expected to align with those strategic priorities and reporting frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spend-down / lifespan policy for the foundation/trust
rubrics_metrics.description: The foundation/trust announced plans to spend all of its resources within a set period after the founders' deaths — originally within 50 years, later lowered to within 20 years — and in May 2025 Bill Gates announced that the foundation will cease operations on December 31, 2045.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This spend-down policy is a strategic constraint shaping long-term grantmaking, intended to reduce administrative overhead over time and ensure funds are directed to charitable causes rather than accumulating for administrative costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of the Trust and Foundation (operational vs. asset management)
rubrics_metrics.description: In October 2006 the organization was split into two entities: the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation Trust, which manages the endowment assets, and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, which "... conducts all operations and grantmaking work, and it is the entity from which all grants are made."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This governance/structural arrangement implies distinct criteria and responsibilities: the Trust manages investments and delivers funds; the Foundation sets programmatic criteria and issues grants. The article lists trust investments to illustrate transparency of major holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant confidentiality / safety exclusion for reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishing grant information (e.g., via IATI or public grant database), the foundation excludes grants that, if published, could harm employees, grantees, partners, or the beneficiaries of its work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a transparency-vs-safety tradeoff: the foundation reports many grants publicly but withholds specific items for confidentiality/security reasons; potential applicants should expect some grants and partners to be omitted from public reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology outcomes expectation for sanitation investments (Omni-Processor example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanitation technology investments often aim for concrete resource-recovery outcomes — e.g., the Omni-Processor aims to convert excreta/fecal sludge into beneficial products such as energy and drinking water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects are evaluated for potential to create local business/revenue models, scalability, and health/safety outcomes; prototype examples (combustion-based systems, electrochemical disinfection, solar-heat treatment) show the kinds of technical performance and downstream benefits expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive scholarship selection statistics (Gates Cambridge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gates Cambridge Scholarship accepts less than 0.3% of applicants; each year approximately 100 new graduate students worldwide receive funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This communicates selectivity and scale for scholarship-type awards administered by the foundation; applicants should expect highly competitive selection and substantial endowment-supported awards.
